name: hevea
why: LaTeX-to-HTML translator written in OCaml; an unusual old-school tool worth a look at how it parses TeX.

brief.what_it_is: HEVEA is a LaTeX-to-HTML translator written in OCaml. It takes LaTeX source (a fairly complete subset of LaTeX2e, and old-style LaTeX is also accepted) and writes HTML, aiming at HTML5. Exotic symbols become HTML entities that reference Unicode characters. The whole document comes out as a single HTML file, which the companion program HACHA can split into smaller pages. The distribution installs hevea, hacha, bibhva, esponja and imagen.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says HEVEA is a fast tool for translating large documents such as manuals and books into HTML, and that simple user style files are understood with little or no modification. Customisation is done by writing LaTeX code rather than a separate configuration language.
brief.how_it_works: The README says HEVEA understands LaTeX macro definitions and is written in OCaml, "as many lexers" are. Its output is one single HTML file, which HACHA can cut into smaller files. The sources and README do not describe the parsing internals in detail; the homepage links to a French article on the implementation, which I did not fetch.

brief.install_notes: Via opam: opam update, then opam install hevea. From source: install OCaml and ocamlbuild (opam is suggested), download the v2.38 tarball, then run make and make install. Before building, you can edit the Makefile: TARGET=opt (the default, native code, about three times faster) or TARGET=byte if only ocamlc is available; LIBDIR defaults to /usr/local/lib/hevea; BINDIR defaults to /usr/local/bin. The hevea.sty file is only copied to LIBDIR, so making it visible to LaTeX is the user's job. Optional extras are a modern LaTeX with dvips, Ghostscript and netpbm; HEVEA runs without them. A Windows (Win32) port by Philip A. Viton exists, and the homepage says it is on MacPorts and many Linux package systems.
brief.standout: It is an older, pre-LaTeX3 style tool that reads TeX-style macro definitions and emits a single HTML file, with HACHA as a separate splitter. The author describes it as a fast lexer-based program in OCaml, and it was used to translate 14 documents by 14 different authors.
brief.status: Maintained, as far as the evidence goes. The homepage and GitHub README both give the current version as 2.38, and the homepage also links to a GitHub repository and a mailing list. I did not find a release date or last-commit date in the pages I read, so the exact recency is unknown.
brief.caveats: The homepage says the source should compile with OCaml 3.12 or later, but the GitHub README says 4.08 or newer is needed; the README is probably the more current statement. HTML 4.01 output needs the frozen version 1.99 instead. The Makefile must be edited for non-default paths. hevea.sty must be made visible to LaTeX by hand. The input is a subset of LaTeX2e, not the whole language. Licensing is the Q Public License for HEVEA itself, with parts of the OCaml runtime under the LGPL; the manual is under the Free Document Dissemination Licence.
quotes: HEVEA is a quite complete and fast LATEX to HTML translator.
Using HEVEA it is possible to translate large documents such as manuals, books, etc. very quickly.
Check for hevea on your package system: no other software has the same name!
